analysis.investment_thesis: Asahi India is a market-leading automotive and architectural glass manufacturer, but a Debt/Equity of 0.77, negative free cash flow for two consecutive years (–INR 244 Cr and –INR 536 Cr), and a P/E of 69x collectively fail every test I apply to a business before writing a cheque. The balance sheet is deteriorating as borrowings have grown from INR 1,238 Cr to INR 2,856 Cr in three years to fund aggressive capex.
key_strengths: Dominant position in Indian automotive glass — structural oligopoly with Japanese-parent technology advantage
Operating margin at 14.2% is the best among these five stocks and has been resilient
Finance costs actually contracting over 9 years (–1.3% CAGR), showing historical discipline
key_risks: Debt/Equity of 0.77 is well above my hard limit of 0.5 — borrowings nearly doubled in two years to fund capex
Free cash flow turned deeply negative: –INR 244 Cr in FY24 and –INR 536 Cr in FY25; capex is INR 1,268 Cr in FY25
P/E of 69.2x and EV/EBITDA of 31.9x price in perfection for a 8.5% revenue CAGR business with 13.6% ROE
red_flags: Debt/Equity at 0.77 — automatic red flag; breaches my 0.5 ceiling firmly
Borrowings exploded from INR 1,238 Cr (FY22) to INR 2,856 Cr (FY25) — aggressive debt-funded expansion
ROE of 13.6% with heavy debt means the equity return is artificially supported by leverage, not business quality
analysis.detailed_analysis:
I have built businesses in retail where tight working capital and low debt were survival requirements, not preferences. Asahi's glass business is structurally attractive — high barriers, technological moat from Asahi Glass Japan — but the current financial trajectory is troubling. Capex went from INR 101 Cr in FY22 to INR 1,268 Cr in FY25, funded almost entirely by debt, with borrowed funds growing from INR 1.2k Cr to INR 2.9k Cr. ROE at 13.6% for a company taking on this leverage is mediocre, and the market is paying 69x earnings for it.

At P/B of 5.86x and P/S of 4.51x, there is no margin of safety. Revenue CAGR over nine years is only 8.5% — I would need 14–15% CAGR to justify double-digit P/E multiples, let alone 69x. The glass business is also cyclically sensitive to the auto cycle and real-estate construction. I would wait for the capex cycle to normalise, debt to reduce, and the price to reflect reality before revisiting.
